Reg E: what Regulation E requires of banks

MT

Mehak Tariq, CAMSNovember 22, 2026•9 min read

Reg E, or Regulation E, is the federal rule that protects consumers who move money electronically: debit card purchases, ATM withdrawals, direct deposits, ACH debits and person-to-person payments from a consumer account. It implements the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and sits at 12 CFR part 1005. For a bank or fintech, Reg E's core duties cover four areas: what to disclose, what to show on receipts and statements, how much a consumer can lose to an unauthorized transfer, and how fast an error notice has to be investigated and answered.

This guide explains public guidance and is not legal advice.

The Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Regulation E

The Electronic Fund Transfer Act (EFTA) dates from 1978. Section 1005.1 says the act establishes "the basic rights, liabilities, and responsibilities" of consumers who use electronic fund transfer and remittance transfer services, and of the institutions that offer them. It names the primary objective as "the protection of individual consumers".

The Federal Reserve Board wrote Regulation E first. The Dodd-Frank Act transferred rulemaking authority under the EFTA to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and in December 2011 the CFPB restated the rule at 12 CFR part 1005, as the Fed's Consumer Compliance Handbook explains. Some authority stayed with the Board. Section 1029 of Dodd-Frank generally kept authority over certain motor vehicle dealers out of the transfer, and the Board's own version of Regulation E is still in the CFR at 12 CFR part 205. Section 920 of the EFTA, on debit card interchange fees, is implemented by the Board at 12 CFR part 235.

What Regulation E applies to

Under section 1005.3, the rule applies to any electronic fund transfer "that authorizes a financial institution to debit or credit a consumer's account". Three definitions in section 1005.2 decide most coverage questions:

  • A consumer is a natural person. Accounts held for business purposes fall outside the account definition below, even when a natural person holds them.
  • An account is a checking, savings or other consumer asset account "established primarily for personal, family, or household purposes". Prepaid accounts, including payroll card accounts, are included.
  • A financial institution is a bank, savings association or credit union, or any other person that holds a consumer's account or "issues an access device and agrees with a consumer to provide electronic fund transfer services".

That last definition is why Reg E reaches fintechs. The CFPB's Electronic Fund Transfers FAQs treat P2P and bill payment providers as financial institutions when they meet it, and P2P payments that meet the definition of an electronic fund transfer as covered.

Covered (examples in 1005.3(b))Excluded (1005.3(c))
Point-of-sale transfersTransfers originated by check, draft or similar paper
ATM transfersCheck guarantee or authorization services
Direct deposits and withdrawalsFedwire and similar wire systems used mainly between institutions or businesses
Transfers initiated by telephoneTransfers whose main purpose is buying or selling regulated securities or commodities
Debit card transactions, at a terminal or notCertain automatic transfers inside the account-holding institution, and telephone transfers made outside a bill-payment or other written plan
One-time transfers using information from a checkPreauthorized transfers at institutions with $100 million or less in assets on the preceding December 31

Paper checks stay outside Reg E, which is why check fraud controls such as positive pay run under different rules.

Consumer liability for unauthorized transfers

An unauthorized transfer is one initiated by someone other than the consumer "without actual authority" and from which the consumer receives no benefit. The definition excludes transfers by someone the consumer gave the access device to (until the consumer tells the institution that person is no longer authorized), transfers made with the consumer's fraudulent intent, and transfers by the institution or its employee. The official interpretations in Supplement I add that this includes a transfer by someone who got the access device "through fraud or robbery". The CFPB FAQs apply the same reading to a consumer who was tricked into sharing login details or a one-time code. Our guide to account takeover fraud prevention covers the controls that stop those transfers before they happen.

Section 1005.6 caps what the consumer can be made to pay, based on how fast they report:

When the consumer reportsMost the consumer can be liable for
Within two business days of learning a card or other access device was lost or stolenThe lesser of $50 or the unauthorized transfers before notice
After those two business daysThe lesser of $500 or the sum of $50 (or the transfers in the first two business days, if less) and later transfers before notice that the institution shows timely notice would have prevented
More than 60 days after the statement showing the transfer was sentTransfers after the 60 days and before notice, if the institution shows timely notice would have stopped them, plus any amount under the rows above if an access device was involved

For example, a consumer reports a stolen debit card a week after learning of the theft. $40 was taken in the first two business days and $860 after. If the institution shows timely notice would have stopped the $860, the consumer owes at most $500.

Three limits apply to the institution. It can only hold the consumer liable if it gave the liability, contact and business-day disclosures in 1005.7(b)(1) to (3) and, where an access device was used, the device was accepted and the institution provided a way to identify the consumer. It must extend the time limits to a reasonable period when the delay was due to "extenuating circumstances". And negligence does not count: the commentary says writing the PIN on the card "does not affect the consumer's liability".

Error notices and investigation deadlines

Section 1005.11 defines an error broadly. It covers unauthorized transfers, incorrect transfers, transfers missing from a statement, bookkeeping mistakes, the wrong amount of cash from an electronic terminal such as an ATM, and a consumer's request for documentation or clarification. A notice counts if it arrives within 60 days after the institution sent the statement first showing the problem, lets the institution identify the consumer's name and account number, and says why the consumer thinks there is an error. It can be oral or written.

  • Investigate and decide within 10 business days, report the result within three business days of finishing, and correct a confirmed error within one business day.
  • If more time is needed, the institution can take up to 45 days from receipt of the notice, provided it provisionally credits the account within 10 business days and tells the consumer within two business days of crediting.
  • The 10 days become 20 business days for transfers within 30 days after the first deposit to a new account. The 45 days become 90 days for transfers not initiated in a state, point-of-sale debit card transactions, and transfers within 30 days after the first deposit.

An institution may ask for written confirmation of an oral notice within 10 business days, but under the commentary it "may not delay until it has received a written confirmation" before starting the investigation.

Disclosures and Reg E statement requirements

Section 1005.7 requires initial disclosures when the consumer contracts for the service or before the first transfer, including the liability summary, who to call about unauthorized transfers, fees, stop payment rights and an error resolution notice. Section 1005.8 adds 21 days' notice before changes that raise fees or liability, cut transfer types or tighten transfer limits, plus an error resolution notice at least once a year or an abbreviated one with each statement.

Section 1005.9 covers receipts and statements. Terminal receipts are required for transfers over $15. A periodic statement goes out for each monthly cycle with a transfer, and at least quarterly otherwise. It must show each transfer's amount, date, type and third party, the account number, fees, opening and closing balances, and the address and phone number for questions, "preceded by 'Direct inquiries to' or similar language".

Other Reg E banking rules to know

  • Preauthorized debits need a written authorization "signed or similarly authenticated by the consumer", and a copy goes to the consumer (1005.10).
  • Consumers can stop a preauthorized debit by notifying the institution at least three business days before the scheduled date. An oral stop payment order lapses after 14 days if written confirmation is required and does not arrive.
  • No institution may require repayment of credit by preauthorized transfer, with exceptions such as overdraft credit plans, or require an account at a particular institution as a condition of a job or government benefit.
  • An institution cannot charge an overdraft fee on ATM or one-time debit card transactions unless the consumer has opted in after a segregated notice (1005.17).
  • Prepaid accounts (1005.18) and gift cards (1005.20) have their own sections.

How a bank or fintech team runs Reg E

A procedure that meets those deadlines on every notice can run in seven steps:

  1. Map coverage. Mark which products are consumer accounts and which payment types are electronic fund transfers.
  2. Check the documents. Confirm disclosures, error notices, statement fields and change-in-terms timing match the sections above.
  3. Take notices from every channel: calls, chat, branches, email and the app. Log the date received, since the clock starts there.
  4. Set the clock per notice. Record the statement date, new-account status, transfer type and the resulting 10- or 20-business-day and 45- or 90-day limits.
  5. Investigate without waiting on the consumer. Pull the transfer record and login data; fraud alert review often holds the same facts.
  6. Decide liability. Apply the 1005.6 tiers to the reporting dates, and record why any amount is withheld.
  7. Report and close. Send the result, correct within one business day, and on a denial send the written explanation and offer the documents.

The CFPB FAQs describe practices that examiners or an enforcement action found unlawful: requiring a police report or other documents before starting an investigation, telling the consumer to contact the merchant first, and applying network rules that give less protection, such as a 60-day window counted from the transaction date instead of the statement date. The FAQs also cite the EFTA's anti-waiver section: no agreement with a consumer can waive these rights. Track repeat issues through complaints triage. If your team writes this procedure down, Verkflo can run it as a versioned agent workflow that pauses for an analyst's decision and records each step in its audit log.

Record retention

Section 1005.13 requires "evidence of compliance" for at least two years from the date disclosures are required or action is required to be taken, and until final disposition when it has actual notice of an investigation or enforcement proceeding, or has been served notice of a lawsuit under the act.

Common questions

Does Reg E apply to business accounts?

No. The rule protects consumers, defined as natural persons, and covers accounts established primarily for personal, family or household purposes.

Does Regulation E apply to P2P payments?

The CFPB's FAQs say a P2P payment that meets the definition of an electronic fund transfer is covered, including credit-push payments out of a consumer account, and that a transfer made by a fraudster with credentials obtained by theft or trickery is unauthorized.

Is the CFPB or the Fed responsible for Reg E?

The CFPB writes the rule at 12 CFR part 1005. The Fed keeps 12 CFR part 205 and the debit interchange rules at part 235. Which agency examines an institution depends on its size and charter.
